strengths: Comprehensive system-level contribution combining automated tool-augmented data synthesis, agentic RL, and an efficient asynchronous training infrastructure, with concrete quantitative evidence for each component (4-5x speedup in Table 6, ablation of each refinement stage in Table 3, partial rollout segment analysis in Table 7).

Very strong empirical results across four model scales (1.7B, 8B, 30B-A3B, 235B-A22B) on challenging competition benchmarks (AIME24/25, HMMT25) with a clear protocol (avg@32, Math-Verify, consistent inference parameters).

Useful ablations and analyses: SFT vs. RL comparisons with text-only data (Table 2), multi-stage RL budget expansion (Figure 3), dataset scaling from 2k to 300k (Figure 7), and a detailed scaling/refinement pipeline in the appendix including prompts.
Good coverage of related work and baselines, with a large comparison table spanning tool-augmented and text-only models across many sizes.

Well-motivated engineering contributions (request-level async rollout, agentic partial rollout, prefix-aware load balancing) that address a real bottleneck for long-horizon, tool-intensive agent RL, supported by measured latency breakdowns.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely integrative: the method combines existing techniques (GRPO, DAPO tricks, code-interpreter SFT, synthetic CoT-to-code injection similar to prior work such as ReTool/CoRT/START), and the systems techniques echo established asynchronous RL systems (e.g., AReal); the paper does not sharply delineate what is fundamentally new versus re-engineered.

Headline 'state-of-the-art' claims are somewhat overstated: AgentMath-30B-A3B starts from Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 (87.7/85.0/71.4), so the incremental gain is ~2-4 points, and on HMMT25 it ties OpenReasoning-Nemotron-32B (73.8). The 235B-SFT variant remains below Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 (93.4/90.8/81.7 vs 94.2/92.3/83.9). The contribution of tool augmentation versus a stronger base model's text reasoning is not fully disentangled.

Evaluation is limited to three AIME/HMMT-style benchmarks; no results on broader benchmarks (e.g., MATH-500, Omni-MATH, non-competition distributions), raising concerns about generalization and about whether competition-specific filtering/synthesis biases the results. Contamination mitigation is described but only n-gram/MinHash/semantic filtering, which is imperfect for these saturated benchmarks.
No statistical significance analysis or error bars for avg@32 results, and several comparisons rest on small margins (~1-3 points) where differences may not be meaningful.

Incomplete/placeholder sections weaken the submission: A.4 (partial rollout algorithm) and A.5.5 (detailed results) are empty, the conclusion misstates HMMT25 accuracy (78.9% vs 73.8%), and there is no stated plan for code/data release, limiting reproducibility for such a heavily engineered system.

The key RL-versus-baseline comparison (Table 2) is conducted only on Qwen3-8B at 20k SFT data; no controlled RL ablation at larger scales, and the tool-usage reward (Rtool) hyperparameters (alpha, beta, Rmax) are not analyzed, making the reward design claims hard to verify.

strengths: Strong empirical results on challenging competition benchmarks (AIME24/25, HMMT25) across multiple model scales (1.7B to 235B), with the 30B-A3B variant competitive with much larger models.

The systems contribution is substantive: request-level asynchronous rollout scheduling, agentic partial rollout, and prefix-aware weighted load balancing yield a measured 4-5x training speedup, and the ablations (Tables 6-7) supporting these components are convincing and relevant to the agentic RL community.

Reasonably thorough ablation suite: tool-augmented vs. text-only SFT/RL comparison (Table 2), progressive refinement analysis (Table 3), backbone generalization (Table 5), partial-rollout segment count study (Table 7), and a data scaling curve (Figure 7).

The automated trajectory synthesis pipeline (code injection, executability verification, feedback alignment, self-correction injection) is a practical and reusable recipe, and prompts are provided in the appendix, aiding reproducibility of the data methodology.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core recipe (tool-augmented SFT data synthesis + GRPO/DAPO-style RL with interleaved code execution) closely follows existing work such as ReTool, START, ToRL, rStar2-Agent, and AREAL; individual techniques (async scheduling, partial rollout, KL removal, clip-higher) are largely adapted from prior systems rather than new algorithmic contributions.

The headline 'outperforming frontier open-source models' claims are weakened by the starting points: AgentMath-30B-A3B builds on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, which already scores 87.7/85.0/71.4; the absolute gain from the proposed method is only about +3/+1.4/+2.4 points, and the 235B variant is SFT-only, so it cannot attribute the largest-scale results to the RL contribution at all. Comparisons against models trained from weaker bases overstate the contribution.

Possible confound of distillation/contamination: all training corpora derive from DeepSeek-R1-0528 and related distilled sources, and although n-gram/MinHash/semantic filtering is described, the paper does not report any contamination analysis of benchmark-level gains against this heavy distillation lineage.

Manuscript quality issues undermine confidence: Appendix A.4 (the promised partial-rollout algorithm) and A.5.5 are empty; the case-study sections A.8.1/A.8.2 have empty bodies in the text of the appendix; the conclusion misreports HMMT25 accuracy as 78.9% versus 73.8% in the abstract and tables; several references are malformed or mismatched. These suggest a rushed submission.

Evaluation is narrow (three math-competition sets) and protocol consistency with the reported baseline numbers (largely taken from MathArena or papers under differing sampling budgets) is not verified; no out-of-domain evaluation (e.g., general reasoning, code, GSM/Hard benchmarks) is provided to assess whether tool-use training generalizes or just optimizes the target distribution.

The tool-usage reward R_tool = min(R_max, alpha + beta*N_code) monotonically rewards more code invocations up to a cap, which conflicts with the paper's stated goal of 'efficient computational resource utilization' and could incentivize gratuitous tool calls; no ablation isolates the effect of this reward shaping on final performance or call counts.

Reproducibility is questionable in practice: the method relies on frontier teacher models (DeepSeek-V3-0324, R1-0528), a 128-node sandbox cluster, and verl-based infrastructure; no code, data, or model release is mentioned.

strengths: Strong empirical results: AgentMath models achieve state-of-the-art tool-augmented performance at 1.7B, 8B, and 30B-A3B scales on AIME24/25 and HMMT25, with the 30B-A3B variant competitive with much larger frontier models.

Comprehensive system contribution spanning the full pipeline: automated tool-augmented data synthesis with multi-stage quality refinement, agentic RL with loss masking and adaptive batch construction, and an asynchronous training infrastructure (request-level scheduling, partial rollout, prefix-aware load balancing) achieving a credible 4-5x measured speedup.

Good ablation coverage: progressive data refinement steps (Table 3), data scaling from 2k to 300k (Figure 7), tool-augmented vs. text-based SFT/RL comparison (Table 2, Figures 4-5), partial rollout segment count (Table 7), and per-component efficiency breakdown (Table 6).

Reasonable decontamination effort for training data (n-gram, MinHash LSH, semantic similarity filtering against evaluation sets) and a detailed MDP/protocol formulation with implementation details in the appendix.
Interesting analysis of emergent behaviors, including code self-correction and the relationship between tool-call budget/capacity expansion and accuracy gains during multi-stage RL.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the framework is largely a well-executed integration of existing techniques (GRPO/DAPO tricks, ReTool-style tool-integrated reasoning, asynchronous RL infrastructures similar to AReaL). Individual components are incremental; the main novelty is in scale and system engineering.

Narrow evaluation scope: only three math competition benchmarks (AIME24/25, HMMT25, each ~30 problems) are used. No MATH-500, no out-of-domain generalization (code, science, general reasoning), no variance/significance reporting on such small test sets, raising overfitting concerns.

Comparison fairness concerns: baselines are numbers compiled from other papers under heterogeneous settings; the model is evaluated with a very generous budget (96k tokens, 96 tool calls, avg@32) that most baselines do not enjoy, and gains over the closest text-only baselines (e.g., OpenReasoning-Nemotron-32B at 73.8% HMMT25 vs. AgentMath's 73.8%) are sometimes marginal.

Residual contamination risk: the SFT corpus is distilled from DeepSeek-R1-0528-style responses, which themselves may encode benchmark solutions; n-gram/semantic filtering cannot fully rule out leakage, and this is not discussed as a limitation.

Internal inconsistencies and sloppiness: the conclusion reports 78.9% HMMT25 while tables/abstract report 73.8%; sections A.5.5, A.8.1, A.8.2 and A.4 are empty or stub; multiple typos ('Thininking', 'pipline'); low-resolution figures; reward hyperparameters (alpha, beta, Rmax) and several settings are unspecified.

The self-correction case study (Figure 9) is problematic: the demonstrated code computes with a 5th root of unity where the problem requires a 13th root, yet the trace is presented as a successful self-correction example, and the leap to P=8321 is unexplained — this undercuts the 'emergent self-correction' claim.

Reproducibility is limited: the training setup (128-node sandbox cluster, 316k synthetic trajectories, large-scale RL on MoE models) is far beyond typical academic resources, and no code/data release is mentioned.

strengths: Comprehensive training pipeline spanning automated tool-augmented data synthesis (code injection, executability verification, feedback alignment, self-correction injection), agentic RL, and a scalable asynchronous RL infrastructure (request-level scheduling, partial rollout, prefix-aware load balancing) with a well-documented 4-5x speedup decomposition (Table 6).

Strong empirical results across model scales (1.7B to 235B-A22B), with thorough ablations: data refinement pipeline (Table 3), scaling laws for SFT and RL data (Tables 18-19), reward design grid search (Table 27), partial rollout segment count (Table 7), teacher model selection, and controlled comparison against ReTool under identical configurations (Tables 25-26).

Substantial attention to evaluation rigor: multi-stage decontamination (n-gram + MinHash + semantic filtering), supplementary evaluation on the post-hoc Google-IMO-AnswerBench, and temporal controls using base models released before benchmark publication (Tables 13-17), which addresses contamination concerns proactively.
Extensive documentation of prompts, MDP formulation, reward design, and hyperparameters, supporting reproducibility; the work is also positioned as a resource for the open-source community.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: each component is a combination of existing techniques (GRPO/DAPO tricks, tool-integrated reasoning as in ToRA/START/ReTool/CoRT, asynchronous partial rollouts similar to prior systems like AReaL and RollPacker). The contribution is primarily a well-engineered integration and scaling study rather than a fundamentally new method.

Small evaluation benchmarks: AIME24/25 and HMMT25 contain only ~30 problems each, making large gaps hard to interpret statistically; while IMO-AnswerBench is added, the headline SOTA claims rest mainly on these tiny test sets, and avg@32 (or avg@8) results are reported without confidence intervals or significance testing.

Comparison fairness concerns: AgentMath is evaluated with 96k-token contexts and up to 96 tool calls, whereas many baseline numbers are taken from prior papers or MathArena under different (often more constrained) inference budgets; a matched-budget re-evaluation of key baselines is not provided. Some baselines are also text-only models being compared to a tool-augmented system.

Manuscript polish issues suggest an incomplete submission: the conclusion reports 78.9% on HMMT25 contradicting the 73.8% in abstract and Table 1; several appendix sections (A.4 Agentic Partial Rollout Algorithm, A.5.5 Detail Results, A.8.1/A.8.2 case studies) are empty headings; duplicate/placeholder citations and typos appear throughout (e.g., 'Frontier Models (1B ~ 2B)', 'pipline', 'Thininking').

Despite the reproducibility statement, no code, data, or model release link is provided in the submission; the open-sourcing claim is only prospective, weakening reproducibility claims at review time.

The SFT corpus is built on responses distilled from DeepSeek-R1-0528 and synthesized by DeepSeek-V3, so part of the gains over purely open baselines may stem from stronger teacher distillation; the controlled AM-Thinking comparison partially addresses this but only at the 8B SFT scale.

strengths: Comprehensive experimental coverage: results across four model scales (1.7B to 235B) on AIME24/25 and HMMT25, with extensive comparisons against both tool-augmented and text-only frontier models, and avg@32 evaluation for robustness.

Unusually thorough ablation suite for this type of paper: segment-length analysis (Table 20), code complexity filtering statistics (Table 21), reward design grid search (Table 27), partial rollout segment counts (Table 7), SFT/RL data scaling (Tables 18-19), and a controlled head-to-head comparison with ReTool under identical settings (Table 25).

Serious effort on decontamination and benchmark reliability: a three-stage dedup pipeline (exact, MinHash/4-gram, semantic embedding), evaluation on a post-hoc uncontaminated benchmark (IMO-AnswerBench), and validation using base models released before benchmark publication (Tables 14-17). This directly addresses the main credibility concern for AIME-style evaluations.

Fairness analysis of teacher-model distillation (A.15), explicitly controlling for teacher effects when comparing against ReTool and AM-Thinking, which preempts the most common objection to distillation-heavy pipelines.

The systems contribution (request-level async scheduling, agentic partial rollout, prefix-aware load balancing, 4-5x measured speedup in Table 6/11) is concretely quantified and practically relevant for large-scale agentic RL training, where rollout long-tail is a real bottleneck.
Prompts, data construction details, and training hyperparameters are documented in sufficient depth to support reproduction, and the authors commit to open-sourcing the pipeline.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the RL algorithm is GRPO+DAPO (dynamic sampling, clip-higher, KL removal), loss masking of environment tokens is standard, and asynchronous scheduling/partial rollout closely resemble prior systems (AReaL, Rollpacker, ReTool). The core contribution is an integration/engineering effort rather than new learning principles.

The claim of 'emergent' code self-correction is undermined by the method itself: self-correction trajectories are explicitly injected into SFT data via templated teacher prompts (A.6.1), and the case study in Figure 9 reproduces the exact 'Oops, the code above appears to be throwing an error' transition sentence from the template. This is imitation of injected data, not emergence.

The showcased self-correction case study (Figure 9) is internally suspect: the model code comments 'primitive 5th root of unity' and iterates only 5 terms for a product over 13th roots of unity, yet the trajectory concludes with the correct answer via an unverifiable leap ('Thus P=8321'). Presenting this as a demonstration of reliable tool-augmented reasoning weakens confidence.

Internal inconsistencies: the conclusion states 90.6%/86.4%/78.9% for AgentMath-30B-A3B while Table 1 reports 73.8% on HMMT25; Table 3 omits the 'tool-usage rationality assessment' step that appears in Table 9's refinement list; average tool calls per sample is reported as 8.3 in one place and 5.1-6.5 in another. These reduce trust in the reported numbers.

Dependence on very small evaluation sets (~30 problems each for AIME24/25, HMMT25) means headline gains of a few points are statistically fragile even with avg@32, and the strongest results rely on a heavily distilled 30B MoE model initialized from Qwen3-Instruct-2507, complicating attribution of gains to the proposed method alone.

The tool-usage reward (conditioned on correctness, rewarding more tool calls) partially incentivizes the very behavior the tool-rationality filtering tries to prevent, and the interaction between these opposing forces is not analyzed.

Writing quality issues (e.g., 'scenarios with scenarios with', inconsistent notation, duplicated reference entries, Figure 1 labeling) and heavy reliance on appendix material for core contributions (A.10 essentially duplicates the introduction) hurt clarity.

strengths: Comprehensive system contribution covering the full pipeline: automated tool-augmented trajectory synthesis, agentic RL, and scalable training infrastructure, with strong empirical results across model scales (1.7B to 235B) on AIME24/25 and HMMT25.

The systems-level contributions (request-level asynchronous rollout scheduling, agentic partial rollout, prefix-aware weighted load balancing) are concrete, well-motivated by long-tail latency analysis, and quantified (4-5x speedup, Table 6/11; segment count ablation Table 7).

Unusually thorough ablation and analysis: progressive data refinement ablation (Tables 3/9), data scaling laws for both SFT and RL (Tables 10/18/19), teacher model selection (Table 24), reward design grid search (Table 27), and fair controlled comparison against ReTool under identical settings (Tables 8/25).

Proactive and credible contamination analysis: three-stage deduplication (n-gram + MinHash LSH + semantic embedding), temporal controls using base models released before benchmark publication (Llama3.1, Qwen2.5), and evaluation on a recent high-difficulty benchmark (IMO-AnswerBench) that confirms the gains are not artifacts of leakage.

The controlled SFT/RL ablation (Table 2, Figure 4) convincingly isolates the benefit of tool augmentation over text-only training, showing both accuracy gains and ~4x RL training efficiency improvement.
Good reproducibility posture: extensive appendix details on prompts, hyperparameters, data construction, and a reproducibility statement with an open-sourcing commitment.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to prior tool-integrated reasoning work (ReTool, ToRL, START, CoRT): the core idea of interleaving CoT with code execution and RL is established; the main advances are engineering refinements (segmented synthesis, asynchronous rollout) rather than fundamentally new methodology.

Evaluation is confined to three small benchmarks (~30 problems each); avg@32 helps but confidence intervals or significance tests are not reported, and the margins over the strongest competitors (e.g., Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507: 90.6 vs 87.7 on AIME24, and OpenReasoning-Nemotron-32B ties HMMT25 at 73.8) are modest relative to the small test set size.

Comparisons against proprietary models (o3, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-Opus) mix self-reported numbers from public leaderboards under potentially different inference budgets (tool calls, context length, sample counts) with the authors' avg@32 protocol; the tool-use setting for baselines is not always matched, weakening 'SOTA' claims.

Internal inconsistencies undermine polish: the conclusion reports 78.9% HMMT25 for AgentMath-30B-A3B while abstract/Table 1 report 73.8%; several references carry implausible future dates (e.g., 'ICLR 2026', arXiv:2602.13035), suggesting citation errors; the A.4 section (Agentic Partial Rollout Algorithm) is essentially empty in the main appendix despite the algorithm being referenced there.

Some headline claims are under-supported: 'emergent code self-correction capabilities' is illustrated only by two case studies, and the 4-5x speedup is measured on one model/scale configuration without broader validation.

Very heavy compute footprint (128-node sandbox cluster, 300k-sample synthesis, 96k-token RL) raises questions about accessibility and reproducibility for the broader community, and the paper does not report total training cost for the largest models.

The tool-usage reward (R_tool increasing with N_code) is somewhat at odds with the stated goal of tool efficiency and prevents the model from learning to abstain from tools; the justification relies only on small 100-step ablations.
